content:
Hello @all

I would like to ask for feedback on an experimental Lean/Python formalization project that I have been developing with substantial AI assistance.

Repository / review snapshot:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/tree/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity

The project asks a deliberately constrained question:

Given a very small combinatorial provenance structure, what additional mathematical structure can actually be derived without assuming the desired output in the input?

The methodological rule is correspondingly simple:

Do not assume as input what the construction is meant to derive as output.

This is meant quite literally. The project is open-ended: if a proposed structure cannot be derived, if Lean exposes an obstruction, or if finite Python experiments produce a counterexample, that is considered a result and the dependency structure is revised accordingly.

I am posting the project before the later candidate F1/F2 skew-symmetric structure has been formally reached. At this stage I am primarily interested in criticism of the formalization architecture itself, rather than in claims about the later mathematical or physical interpretation.

Current formal state

The snapshot is dated 9 August 2026.

  • Lean 4.31.0

  • derivation DAG: 145 nodes / 401 edges

  • 31 FINISHED / 113 UNFINISHED / 1 ACTIVE

  • formally verified through T002

  • T003 is the current frontier

  • Lean Core: 35 modules

  • Core package: 0 manifest dependencies, 0 mathlib imports

  • separate proof package: 25 source modules, using mathlib@v4.31.0 and the local Core

  • T002: 26 audited declarations, kernel verified

  • no project-local axioms and no sorry in the admitted verified path

  • Python regression layer: 120 tests / 1086 registered subtests PASS

The Core/proof dependency is intentionally one-way:

CNNAProofs (mathlib) ---> CNNA Core (no mathlib)

The Core contains the domain objects, constructive derivation and elementary closure results that can be formulated with Lean/Core alone. More substantial proofs are placed in the separate CNNAProofs package, where mathlib is allowed.

This split is an auditing choice, not a claim that avoiding mathlib is intrinsically desirable. One of the questions I would specifically like feedback on is whether this boundary is useful, excessive, or simply drawn at the wrong places.

What has actually been established so far?

The current verified path reaches a complete recurrent-step interface.

Very roughly, an admissible response-capable state XnX_nXn​, together with its canonical next provenance slot and its coherent record/live state, can be advanced through the current response-coupled construction to a successor Xn+1X_{n+1}Xn+1​.

The important point for the formal architecture is that the successor is proved to re-enter the complete state schema required by the next step, including restoration of the relevant live/state coherence.

Thus recurrence is no longer only something observed in an executable finite implementation; it is now part of the formal interface.

The later F1/F2 structure is not claimed by this snapshot.

Why a DAG?

The derivation is maintained as an explicit directed acyclic graph. Nodes represent primitive inputs, constructions, measurements/cuts, theorems, proof obligations, obstructions, controls and later specializations.

A rule that became increasingly important during the Lean work is:

A missing closure should be proved at the point where the corresponding property originates.

For example, while proving T002, several required facts turned out to belong semantically to earlier constructions such as C004, C005, C006, C007, M001 and M004. Those facts were therefore added and proved at those upstream nodes rather than hidden as convenient local lemmas inside T002.

The intention is that the DAG records not merely execution order, but also proof ownership and provenance of assumptions.

The yEd/GraphML DAG is included in the snapshot:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/blob/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/derivation/registry/dag/DAG_yEd.graphml

Four complementary representations

The project is intentionally not maintained as Lean code alone.

Lean
Kernel-checked deduction for claims that have been formalized.

Python
Finite construction, regression testing, numerical exploration and counterexample search. Finite evidence is not treated as universal proof.

Documentation
Semantic intent, interfaces, interpretation boundaries and proof obligations.

DAG / registry
Dependencies, proof ownership, status, obstructions, source hashes and the current research frontier.

One purpose of this separation is to make two different errors harder to commit:

  1. treating stable numerical behaviour as a proof;

  2. treating a kernel-checked theorem as scientifically interesting merely because it is formally valid.

AI-assisted workflow

AI assistance is explicit rather than hidden.

My role is primarily to determine the research question, admissibility constraints, hypotheses, resets, interpretation and what is allowed to count as an input.

ChatGPT has been used extensively for structural search, cross-domain connections, Lean/Python implementation and proof construction. Claude has been used as an additional review/coherence partner.

Python provides executable finite evidence and Lean provides kernel-checked deduction.

LLM output itself is not considered evidence merely because an LLM produced it.

A somewhat unusual consequence is that the repository is also intentionally machine-readable enough that the complete snapshot can be supplied to an LLM and explored as a connected artifact containing code, DAG, documentation, hashes, proof status and open obligations. This is intended as an additional navigation interface, not as a replacement for ordinary human-readable documentation.

A more detailed description of these roles is here:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/blob/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/community/AI_AND_RESEARCH_WORKFLOW.md

What I would particularly like reviewed

I would be grateful for critical feedback on questions such as:

  1. Is the Lean implementation reasonably idiomatic and correctly layered?

  2. Is the separation between the mathlib-free Core and CNNAProofs sensible?

  3. Are any intended outputs already hidden in types, constructors, imported abstractions or interface assumptions?

  4. Are the closure theorems genuinely informative, or are some merely elaborate restatements of definitions?

  5. Does proof ownership in the DAG make mathematical sense?

  6. Are the Python evidence layer and Lean universal claims kept sufficiently distinct?

  7. Is the repository understandable and reviewable without relying on an LLM?

  8. Where should standard Lean/mathlib abstractions replace local infrastructure?

  9. Which parts should be simplified before another mathematical layer is built on top of this one?

In particular, criticism that finds an assumption that has been smuggled in too early would be extremely useful, because avoiding precisely that is one of the main purposes of the exercise.

Short review note

For a compact overview of the architecture and motivation:

Markdown

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/blob/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/community/COMMUNITY_OVERVIEW.md

PDF

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/blob/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/community/COMMUNITY_OVERVIEW.pdf

The snapshot entry point is:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/blob/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/README.md

The exact current-state metadata can be found here:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/blob/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/CURRENT_STATE.json

The Lean package/audit entry point is:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/tree/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/derivation/code/lean

and the current derivation DAG/registry is here:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/tree/main/Snapshots/20260809_LeanCommunity/derivation/registry

Reproducing the formal audit

From the snapshot:

cd derivation/code/lean
./audit/run_package_boundary_audit.sh --build

For the Python regression suite:

cd derivation/code/python
python -m pytest

Papers and project status

The main paper and supplementary material included in the snapshot remain explicitly marked DRAFT.

The project should therefore not be read as presenting a completed physical theory, nor as claiming that the later target structures necessarily emerge.

The present claim is considerably narrower:

There is now a formally checked derivation path from the primitive finite provenance construction through a recurrent response-coupled state transition, and I would like to know whether the way that path has been modeled and verified in Lean is sound, transparent and worth extending.

There is also an older exploratory snapshot from July which goes substantially further mathematically, but it predates the present proof/provenance discipline. I therefore regard the 20260809 Lean-community snapshot as the current formal claim boundary.

Any criticism of the Lean architecture, theorem interfaces, hidden assumptions, proof organization or use of existing abstractions would be very welcome.

Thanks in advance!
antaris

Addititional historical context: from the “as-is” state to the “to-be” derivation

For context, an older exploratory state of the project is still available here:

https://github.com/antaris82/CNNA-Project/tree/main/Snapshots/20260717

This snapshot represents almost the last substantial as-is state before the current reconstruction. It already reaches much further into the intended mathematical development, but it also exposed several structural problems: the scope of the paper had become too broad, a number of mathematical claims were not yet backed by corresponding formal proofs, and the overall derivation had grown in a way that made the logical dependency chain difficult to inspect.

A version of the paper based on this earlier development was submitted to Preprints.org. One of the central problems identified in the rejection was precisely that the conceptual and mathematical “red thread” through the construction was not sufficiently visible.

Rather than continuing to add results to that structure, I therefore treated the 20260717 state as legacy research code and used it as a source from which to reconstruct the dependency structure explicitly.

The result was the derivation DAG: the old implementation became the as-is state, while the DAG describes the intended to-be derivation. The current project is now being rebuilt node by node along that DAG, with each dependency, assumption, proof obligation, obstruction and interface made explicit.

This is why the current formally verified snapshot appears to reach less far mathematically than the 20260717 snapshot. The difference is intentional:

exploratory as-is state (20260717)
            |
            | extract dependencies, assumptions,
            | obstructions and intended derivation
            v
      to-be derivation DAG
            |
            | rebuild node by node
            | Python + Lean + documentation
            v
current formally verified frontier

The older snapshot therefore shows where the search had already gone. The current project is intended to show, much more rigorously, which parts of that path can actually be derived, in what order, from which assumptions, and with which proof status.
